chapters.title: Chapter 2: Yield Measures and What They Really Mean

lessons.title: The Reinvestment Assumption Hidden Inside Every YTM

children.text: Buy a 10-year G-Sec at an 8% yield, hold it to maturity, get every rupee on time from the Government of India, and you will earn 8% a year. Right? Only if you do something with every coupon that almost nobody does: reinvest it, immediately, at exactly 8%, for the rest of the bond's life. Spend the coupons, or park them in a savings account, and your real return will be meaningfully lower than the YTM you bought at. This lesson exposes the assumption buried inside every YTM and shows you how much it is worth in rupees.

body.text: YTM is a promise with a condition attached: you earn it only if every coupon is reinvested at the YTM itself. What you do with the coupons is part of your return, and over ten years it can be a third of it.

children.text: Where the Assumption Comes From

Look again at the YTM equation. It discounts every cash flow at the same rate. Discounting at a rate and compounding at that rate are the same operation run in opposite directions. So when the equation says a ₹40,000 coupon received in year 2 is worth a certain amount today at 8%, it is quietly assuming that the ₹40,000, once received, keeps growing at 8% until maturity. If it grows at less, the bond delivers less than the YTM said.
Worked Example: ₹10 Lakh in an 8% G-Sec for Ten Years

markDefs.definition: Interest earned by reinvesting coupon payments. Also called interest on interest or coupon reinvestment income.

children.text: Anand Kapoor, a 45-year-old IT consultant in Gurugram, invests ₹10 lakh in an illustrative 10-year G-Sec with an 8% coupon, bought at par, so its YTM is exactly 8%. He receives ₹40,000 every six months, 20 times, and ₹10 lakh back at the end. For him to end up with the wealth an 8% return implies, the bond's total return has three sources: the ₹10 lakh principal, the ₹8 lakh of coupons, and the
interest on interest
those coupons earn once reinvested.

body.caption: The wealth Anand must end up with for his return to truly be 8% a year, compounded half-yearly.

children.text: And the interest on interest does not build evenly. It compounds, so it starts tiny and snowballs. After two years it is under ₹10,000. By year ten it is almost half the size of the coupons themselves.

body.title: Cumulative Coupons vs Interest on Interest at 8% (₹ lakh)
Calculate interest on interest
body.prompt: You buy ₹1 lakh of an illustrative 3-year NCD at par with an 8% annual coupon, paid at the end of each year. You reinvest each coupon at 8% until maturity. How much interest on interest do you earn in total? Round to the nearest rupee.
body.explanation: Year 1 coupon grows for 2 years: ₹8,000 × 1.08² = ₹9,331.20. Year 2 coupon grows for 1 year: ₹8,000 × 1.08 = ₹8,640. Year 3 coupon: ₹8,000. Total coupons with reinvestment = ₹25,971.20, against ₹24,000 of plain coupons, so interest on interest = ₹1,971.20. Check: ₹1,00,000 × 1.08³ = ₹1,25,971.20.

children.text: What Anand Actually Earns at Different Reinvestment Rates

markDefs.definition: The annualised return you actually achieve on a bond held to maturity, based on your real ending wealth including coupons reinvested at the rates you actually got. Also called realised yield.

children.text: The bond pays Anand the same cash flows whatever happens. What changes is what those coupons earn after they land in his account. The honest measure of his outcome is the
realised compound yield
: take the actual ending wealth, and find the annual rate that grows ₹10 lakh into it.

body.caption: Stated on the same half-yearly compounded basis as a G-Sec YTM. N = years held.

body.title: Same Bond, Same 8% YTM, Different Realised Returns

markDefs.definition: The risk that coupons and principal received before your investment horizon have to be reinvested at lower rates than the original yield.

children.text: A default-free Government of India bond, paid in full and on time, can deliver anything from 5.97% to 8.61% depending solely on what happens to the coupons. That uncertainty is
reinvestment risk
, and no credit rating captures it.

body.text: Spending the coupons is not a mistake if you need the income. A retiree living off ₹40,000 every six months is using the bond exactly as intended. Just know that the realised compound yield on that bond will be well below its YTM, and compare it with alternatives on that basis, not on the headline YTM.

children.text: This Is Not Hypothetical: India's 2019 to 2022 Rate Cycle

Investors who locked into bonds yielding 7.5% or more in 2018 learned about reinvestment risk the hard way. Over the next two years RBI cut its policy rate by 250 basis points, and FD rates, savings account rates and new bond yields fell with it. Every coupon those investors received from 2020 to 2022 had to be reinvested at far lower rates than their original YTM.

events.title: Easing cycle begins
events.description: Repo cut from 6.50% to 6.25%, the first of five cuts in 2019.

events.title: Repo at 5.15%

events.title: Pandemic cuts to 4.00%
events.description: Emergency cuts of 75 and 40 basis points take the repo rate to a record low. Coupons are now reinvested at the lowest rates in years.

events.title: Hiking cycle begins
events.description: An unscheduled 40 basis point hike to 4.40% as inflation rises. The repo rate had stayed at 4.00% for two years.

events.title: Repo back at 6.50%
events.description: After hikes through 2022, the repo rate returns to where it started in early 2019. Reinvestment rates recover, but bond prices fell along the way.

children.text: Which Bonds Carry the Most Reinvestment Risk
Reinvestment risk grows with the amount of cash a bond hands back before maturity, and with how long that cash has to be reinvested:
Higher coupon, more risk.
A 9% coupon bond returns more of its value early than a 6% coupon bond, so more of its return depends on reinvestment.
Longer maturity, more risk.
More coupons, each reinvested for longer, so interest on interest becomes a bigger share of the total.
Monthly payout NCDs, more risk still.
Cash arrives twelve times a year, and small monthly amounts are the most likely to sit idle in a savings account.
Zero-coupon bonds, none at all.

T-bills, G-Sec STRIPS and cumulative NCD options pay nothing until maturity. Hold them to the end and the YTM you buy at is exactly the return you get, whatever happens to rates in between (subject, for NCDs, to the issuer paying).

body.title: Rank the risk
body.question: All four illustrative instruments below are bought at a 7.5% YTM and held to maturity. Which one exposes you to the most reinvestment risk?
options: A 3-year NCD with an annual 7.5% coupon
A 10-year NCD paying a 9% coupon monthly
body.explanation: The 10-year monthly-pay NCD combines the three drivers of reinvestment risk: a high coupon, a long maturity and frequent payments. The STRIPS and the T-bill pay nothing until maturity, so they have no reinvestment risk. The 3-year annual NCD has only two coupons to reinvest before maturity.

body.title: Lock in the YTM
body.textWithBlank: A ___ bond held to maturity has no reinvestment risk, because it pays nothing until the end.
body.explanation: With no coupons to reinvest, the only cash flow is the face value at maturity, so the YTM at purchase is exactly the return realised if held to maturity and paid in full.

body.title: The Two Interest Rate Risks Pull in Opposite Directions

columns.label: If rates fall after you buy
points: Bad for reinvestment: coupons earn less when reinvested
Good for price: the bond is worth more if you sell early
Hurts most if you hold to maturity and reinvest every coupon

columns.label: If rates rise after you buy
points: Good for reinvestment: coupons earn more when reinvested
Bad for price: the bond is worth less if you sell early
Hurts most if you have to sell before maturity

children.text: Because these two risks offset each other, there is a holding period at which they roughly cancel out. That period turns out to be the bond's duration, which you will meet in Chapter 3 and use to match bonds to goals in Chapter 5.

body.title: Lakshmi's education fund
body.scenario: Lakshmi Narayanan, a 35-year-old architect in Coimbatore, invests ₹5 lakh on RBI Retail Direct in an illustrative 10-year G-Sec with a 7.20% coupon, bought at par. It is for her daughter's college fees in exactly ten years. She is pleased: "7.2% guaranteed by the Government of India." Her ₹18,000 coupons will be credited every six months to her savings account, which pays about 3% a year, and she plans to leave them there.
body.prompt: Estimate what Lakshmi will actually have in ten years, compare it with what a true 7.20% return would give, and suggest practical ways to close the gap.
body.modelAnswer:
1. A true 7.20% return, compounded half-yearly, would grow ₹5 lakh to ₹5,00,000 × 1.036²⁰ = ₹10,14,297.
2. With coupons earning about 3% a year (1.5% per half-year for simplicity): coupons plus interest = ₹18,000 × (1.015²⁰ − 1) ÷ 0.015 = ₹4,16,226. Adding the ₹5 lakh principal gives ₹9,16,226.
3. Her realised compound yield is about 6.15%, not 7.20%. The shortfall is roughly ₹98,000, almost a fifth of her original investment, entirely from idle coupons.
4. Even reinvesting at 6% a year would give about ₹9,83,667 (6.88%), still short of the YTM outcome.
5. Ways to close the gap: (a) Sweep each coupon into a debt investment yielding close to 7%, such as another G-Sec purchase on RBI Retail Direct or a low-cost gilt or target maturity fund, accepting that future reinvestment rates are not guaranteed. (b) For a fixed goal date, consider a zero-coupon instrument such as G-Sec STRIPS maturing near the goal, which has no reinvestment risk if held to maturity. (c) At minimum, move coupons out of the savings account promptly rather than letting them accumulate.
6. The deeper lesson: the Government of India guarantees the cash flows, not the 7.20% return. The last part of that return is Lakshmi's job.

points: YTM assumes every coupon is reinvested at the YTM itself until maturity. Discounting at one rate implies compounding at that rate.
On ₹10 lakh in a 10-year 8% G-Sec, ₹3.91 lakh of the ₹11.91 lakh gain, 32.8%, comes from interest on interest that the bond never pays.
Realised compound yield measures what you actually earned: 5.97% if coupons are spent, 8.61% if reinvested at 10%.
Reinvestment risk rises with higher coupons, longer maturities and more frequent payouts.
Zero-coupon instruments such as T-bills and STRIPS have no reinvestment risk if held to maturity.
Falling rates hurt reinvestment but help prices; rising rates do the opposite. Duration is the horizon where they balance.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Investors, bonds and reinvestment rates are illustrative, and all figures are before tax and costs. Future reinvestment rates are unknown, and past RBI rate cycles do not predict future ones. Verify instrument details on RBI Retail Direct, NSE, BSE or the relevant scheme documents, and consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser before investing.
